1.pericope_label: The proverbs of Solomon: a wise son maketh a glad father: the hand of the diligent maketh rich

schools.summary: Henry balances the profit of treasure against the loss of wickedness and finds the account will not countervail, observes that what the injustice of men gathers the justice of God scatters, allows the deceitful hand as a reading and applies it to men honest only under observation, and turns the harvest proverb into a parable of youth whose indolence is repaid with shame in old age.

Gill notes the repeated title and the preface that precedes it, holds the sayings for the most part independent of each other and generally antithetic, presses the point that riches cannot redeem a man or put off death by a moment, and reports two alternative renderings of the slack hand, a deceitful hand and, from an interpreter, a deceitful balance.

Clarke declares it impossible to summarise a chapter where almost every verse is a separate subject, reports manuscripts of the Latin that head this place the second book of the Proverbs, names the form of the parallel as the antithetic after a bishop of his own century and grades its degrees from word-for-word opposition down to general disparity, and reports a variant reading of the perfidious for the wicked found in a dozen or so collated manuscripts but in no ancient version; Wesley reads the summer gathering as improving opportunities of doing good.

Ellicott holds that the collector grouped proverbs by subject though the connection is sometimes too slight to catch, argues at length that righteousness here means almsgiving in particular on the evidence of the Greek and of later Hebrew usage, and renders the second half of the third verse of a passionate desire that God repels; Keil and Delitzsch find the collection stamped as a book for youth by its opening proverbs, render the same noun craving rather than substance from a root meaning to gape, and define the slack hand from the body as a throwing of oneself down with unbent muscles.

debates: How coherent is the chapter? Gill holds the sayings for the most part independent of each other; Clarke says it is impossible to summarise a chapter where almost every verse contains a separate subject; Ellicott allows that each verse is distinct and complete but maintains that the collector tried to throw together those touching the same subject, giving two pairs as examples while conceding the connection is sometimes too slight to catch; Keil and Delitzsch find a unity of purpose instead, the opening proverbs stamping the collection as a book for youth.

Does God cast away the substance of the wicked or repel their desire? Keil and Delitzsch render craving rather than substance, from a root meaning to gape, and report that the Greek and one other version wrongly found the sense of life in the word while two others found possession; Ellicott independently renders it the eager passionate desire of the wicked, which God thrusts away; Gill, Henry and Clarke keep substance, Clarke adding a variant that reads the perfidious for the wicked in a dozen or so manuscripts and in no ancient version.

What is the slack hand? Gill reports a deceitful hand and, from an interpreter, a deceitful balance, which would make the proverb about false weights; Henry allows the deceitful hand; Keil and Delitzsch rule the balance out as contrary to biblical usage and define the word bodily, as the throwing of oneself down lazily with unbent muscles.
outliers: Ellicott narrows righteousness in the second verse to almsgiving in particular, on the ground that it stands against riches got by wrong, that its Greek equivalent bears that sense, and that two later books read it so when they quote the line.
Clarke reports that some ancient manuscripts of the Latin head this chapter as the second book of the Proverbs, the preceding nine chapters being only an introduction to the sayings themselves.

Keil and Delitzsch warn against concluding from the separation of father and mother that grief for a wayward son falls chiefly on the mother, holding that the idea of the parents is only distributed between the two members.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the soul in the third verse as the faculty of desire after nourishment, the lowest form of the life of the soul being the impulse to self-preservation.
themes: a book that begins in the middle of a book
righteousness narrowed to almsgiving
substance read as appetite
a slack hand and a false balance
a collection stamped as a book for the young

6.pericope_label: Blessings are upon the head of the just: the memory of the just is blessed: the mouth of a righteous man is a well of life

schools.summary: Henry adopts the imperative reading of the verse on memory as the duty of survivors, switches without comment between having the mouths of the wicked stopped with shame and having them disguise mischief with professions of friendship, offers a second sense of walking surely as caution rather than safety, and turns the well of life into streams that water ground and quench a traveller’s thirst.

Gill reports the Jewish writers taking the verse on memory as a command and abbreviating the blessing to attach it to the names of their celebrated dead, keeps the well of life as a fountain continually running with wholesome water, fills the walking uprightly with a whole Christian life, and takes the head of the just for Christ with a pointed remark about which head of the church he means.

Clarke reports the Greek reading that replaces the repeated clause of the tenth verse with a promise that free reproof makes peace and defends its sense, notes that memory and name are synonymous so that only two antithetic terms stand in that verse, calls the name of the wicked as offensive as putrid carrion, sets two old English renderings of the sixth verse side by side, and derives the well of life from the great aorta; Wesley suggests the covered mouth alludes to the covering of the faces of condemned malefactors.

Keil and Delitzsch read the same clause with violence as subject in the sixth verse and as object in the eleventh, defending the change by the windings characteristic of the proverb form, report the Greek variant in the tenth verse, answer a critic on the ninth by noting that the consonant text is five hundred years older than the accentuation, and observe that the prophets call God the fountain of life whereas the proverb plants the figure on ethical ground; Ellicott reaches the same reading of the eleventh verse by the same argument and offers instruction by misfortune as an alternative to being found out.

debates: Who covers what in the clause about violence and the mouth of the wicked? Keil and Delitzsch keep violence as the thing that covers in the sixth verse, refusing the alternative because it renounces the sharpness of the contrast, and then make violence the thing covered in the eleventh, where the contrast requires it, defending the reversal by the manifold windings characteristic of the proverb form; Ellicott reaches the same two readings by the same reasoning; Henry moves between them without remarking on it; Wesley refers the covering to the ancient custom of covering the faces of condemned men.

Does the tenth verse end as the eighth does? Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch both report that the Greek has instead a promise that he who reproves with freedom makes peace, Clarke adding two further versions that agree and arguing that open reproof does more for the peace of society than passing sin by, while Keil and Delitzsch only note the striking contrast it makes with the first half of the verse.
outliers: Gill reports that the Jewish writers treat the blessing on the memory of the just as a binding precept, abbreviate it to its initial letters, and attach it to the names of their celebrated dead; Keil and Delitzsch confirm the formula and Henry adopts the imperative reading.

Clarke sets two old English versions of the sixth verse side by side, one from his manuscript Bible and one from an early printed version whose text is different altogether, making the forehead of the ungodly past shame and presumptuous.

Clarke derives the well of life from the great aorta carrying blood from the heart to every part of the body, the same anatomical turn he takes elsewhere in this book at the verse about the issues of life.
Keil and Delitzsch answer a critic on the ninth verse by pointing out that the consonant text is at least five hundred years older than the accentuation his argument depends on.
themes: one clause construed two ways in six verses
a blessing abbreviated into a monogram
a variant that turns a threat into a peacemaker
a fountain traced to the great artery
a name left to rot

12.pericope_label: Hatred stirreth up strifes, but love covereth all sins: the rich man’s wealth is his strong city

schools.summary: Henry keeps the covering of sins within human relations, love concealing and extenuating an offence so far as it can be, likens the wise man to a householder bringing out things new and old, and alone treats both halves of the verse on wealth and poverty as mistakes, the rich thinking themselves happy and the poor thinking themselves undone, since a man may live comfortably on little if he is content.

Gill has hatred waking contentions that were happily laid asleep, adds a second sense to the laying up of knowledge, that the wise conceal it and do not boast of it, and hedges the rich man’s strong city by allowing that it is such in his own apprehension and conceit.

Clarke says love pours water and not oil upon the flame, calls the rod a most powerful instrument of knowledge with a lesson of profound wisdom in every twig, reduces the storing of knowledge to a rule of thinking much and speaking little, protests that every rich man becomes rich by means of the poor so that oppressing them is diabolically unjust, holds that a man in abject poverty never rises out of the pit for want of a nucleus about which property may gather, and gives the righteous man two aims, to support life and then to have something to divide with the poor; Wesley notes that fools are more forward to lay out than to lay up.

Keil and Delitzsch define the covering of sins as pardoning, concealing, excusing or restraining them, separate the verse from the apostolic saying that resembles it, refuse two constructions that other commentators adopt in the following verses, weigh an inward against an outward reading of the rich man’s strong city and prefer the outward, find the two nouns of the sixteenth verse deliberately chosen, and settle the seventeenth by accentuation so that there is a way to life rather than a wayfarer to it; Ellicott separates the same apostolic saying, reaches the same phrase for the fool’s mouth, and takes the closing verb as committing error rather than causing others to err.

debates: Is the covering of sins here the same as the apostolic saying about love covering a multitude of sins? Keil and Delitzsch distinguish them, making the covering here a pardoning, concealing, excusing or restraining among men, while the apostolic sense is a covering from the eyes of a holy God, and note that neither apostle took the phrase from any Greek version of this book; Ellicott allows the resemblance but judges the sense probably different; Henry and Clarke keep the verse wholly among neighbours.

How is the verse about the rich man’s wealth to be taken? Keil and Delitzsch set an inward reading, wealth as a consciousness of power and poverty as a timidity easily dejected, against an outward one, wealth as an actual bulwark, and judge the outward allowable and much the nearer; Ellicott offers both without deciding; Gill allows that the strong city may exist only in the rich man’s own conceit; Henry goes further and makes both halves of the verse errors, the rich mistaken in thinking themselves safe and the poor mistaken in thinking themselves undone.
outliers: Clarke turns the proverb about the rich man’s wealth into a protest that there is not a rich man on earth but becomes such by means of the poor, that property comes from their labour and the king himself is served of the field, and that to despise or oppress them is unjust and diabolically so.

Clarke holds that a man in abject poverty never rises out of the pit, having no nucleus about which property may aggregate, and quotes a Latin poet to the effect that those rarely emerge whose exertions are cramped by want at home.

Keil and Delitzsch twice refuse constructions that other commentators adopt, declining to make the rod a second thing found on the lips of the wise because wisdom and a rod found together would be a figure in bad taste, and declining to make the fool’s mouth a house that suddenly falls in.
Clarke calls the rod a most powerful instrument of knowledge and says that, judiciously applied, there is a lesson of profound wisdom in every twig.
themes: love that covers by restraining as well as by pardoning
a proverb read as two mistakes at once
wealth traced back to the labour it came from
a way to life rather than a walker on it
knowledge stored and deliberately not displayed

18.pericope_label: He that hideth hatred with lying lips: in the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: the blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich

schools.summary: Henry answers the verse on many words with a proverb of his own, that little said is soon amended, defines desirable wealth as wealth held with a heart to take the comfort of it, and notices that the word for sport in the last verse is the word behind the name of Isaac, with the fool laughing at the shaking of the spear.

Gill offers both constructions of the first verse and makes the dissembler and the slanderer alike fools, quotes the rabbis on the multitude of words, and denies that the lips feed bodies, since it is not enough to bid the distressed be warmed and filled and give nothing.

Clarke observes how commonly men full of meditated revenge protest that they thought nothing of the injury, states it as an impossibility to speak much and yet speak nothing but truth, turns sarcastic on the worthless heart which a sinner vaunts of because it is his most hidden part, notes that cares come with all property not acquired by blessing, and asks how many lies such men tell in jest to go to the devil in earnest; Wesley says fools have not wisdom to preserve themselves, much less to feed others.

Keil and Delitzsch make the first verse say that he who hides hatred is a mouth of falsehood and refuse the Greek reading that makes righteous lips conceal enmity, reject a narrow sense of the verse on many words and set a Greek saying and a rabbinic maxim beside it, report the Greek and Aramaic variants at the worthless heart, refuse the rendering that makes many fools die through one demented man, deny on a pronoun that the blessing is said to bring no sorrow, and fix the last verse on a word meaning an outrage against morality; Ellicott agrees on the first verse and the last but proposes as an alternative the very rendering they refused.

debates: Does the first verse say that lying lips hide hatred, or that the man who hides hatred is a mouth of falsehood? Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both take the second; Gill offers both without choosing; Keil and Delitzsch additionally refuse a Greek reading that makes righteous lips conceal enmity, preferred by one critic and made the basis of a conjecture by another, arguing that hiding hatred is a different thing from covering sin and that the Greek word is probably a corruption.

Do fools die for want of wisdom, or through one who is destitute of it? Keil and Delitzsch reject the second on the ground that a fool has enough in his own folly and does not need to be drawn into destruction by others; Ellicott proposes it as an alternative, arguing that as one righteous man guides many aright, so one unwise man leads many fools to ruin.

Does the blessing of the Lord add no sorrow, or does toil add nothing to it? Keil and Delitzsch hold that the first would require a different form of the pronoun and take the verse to mean that strenuous self-endeavour adds nothing to what God gives; Ellicott records both senses without choosing; Henry, Clarke and Gill all keep the sorrow, Clarke adding that God’s blessing levies no tax upon the comfort.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch set beside the verse on many words both a Greek saying that much talking has many failures and a rabbinic maxim that whoever multiplies words brings on sin, noting that a Jewish commentator explains the verse by that maxim; Gill quotes the rabbis at the same place.

Keil and Delitzsch draw from the last verse the consequence that sin is sport to the fool and wisdom is sport to the man of understanding, the same word governing both halves; Ellicott renders it exactly so.
Henry notices that the word for sport in the last verse is the word behind the name of Isaac.
Clarke turns sarcastic on the worthless heart, saying that a sinner vaunts of his because it is his most hidden part, and that it is very honest and good, only the devil is in it.
themes: a mouth of falsehood rather than lying lips
one fool who ruins many, or many who ruin themselves
a pronoun that decides who adds the sorrow
sport in both halves of one proverb
a name hidden in a word for laughter

24.pericope_label: As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: the fear of the Lord prolongeth days

schools.summary: Henry states the principle of the fear that arrives in a line borrowed from a psalm, that as is the fear so is the wrath, argues that the slothful are unfit even to carry a message and therefore very unmeet for the ministry, since Christ will not own the sending of sluggards into his harvest, and takes the promise of long life without qualification, adding that the days will be happy as well as many.

Gill keeps the whirlwind as a comparison and works it out at length into the man of sin, the locusts of the bottomless pit and the shouting at the destruction of antichrist, reports an interpreter illustrating the fear that arrives by the builders of the tower who were scattered by the very work raised to prevent it, and guards the promise of long life by the unalterable decrees of God.

Clarke keeps the whirlwind as a tornado that leaves neither branch nor root, explains the vinegar chemically as acid dissolving the alkali of the bone and the smoke as irritating the tender vessels of the eye, and has the wicked man imposing on himself by the hope of mercy until he dies without it; Wesley has the gladness accomplished and turned into enjoyment.

Keil and Delitzsch refuse the comparative sense of the particle in the whirlwind verse that three old versions adopt and read it temporally, note that the vinegar proverb stands out of the series, take the word after the Greek for unripe grapes and call two Latin poets as witnesses on smoke, concede that the promise of long life has the present life in view and that the pious often die early so that its verification moves into eternity, and trace both words for hope to an idea of strained looking; Ellicott reaches the same reading of the whirlwind particle and calls the promise of long life the special blessing of the older covenant.

debates: Is the whirlwind a comparison or a moment? Keil and Delitzsch report three old versions taking the particle comparatively and refuse it, arguing that another word for storm and another order of clauses would have been required, and read it temporally, when the storm sweeps past; Ellicott reaches the same verdict in three words; Gill, Henry and Clarke all keep the comparison, Gill running it out into a whole allegory of persecutors and antichrist.

How is the promise of long life to be squared with experience? Gill limits it in advance to what the unalterable decrees of God allow, so that it means only longer than the man expected or than his constitution promised; Ellicott calls it the special blessing of the older covenant, still often fulfilled in those who live quietly into old age; Keil and Delitzsch concede that it has the present life in view and that the pious often enough die early, and move its verification forward into eternity; Henry alone takes it straight.
outliers: Gill reports an interpreter illustrating the fear that arrives by the builders of the tower, who feared being scattered over the earth and were scattered by the very work they raised to prevent it.
Keil and Delitzsch take the word for vinegar, after the Greek, of unripe grapes, and call two Latin poets as witnesses on smoke, one for its bitterness and one for the tears it draws.

Clarke explains the proverb chemically, the acid softening and dissolving the alkali of the bone until the teeth lose their texture, and the smoke irritating the tender vessels of the eye so as to prevent distinct vision.
Henry infers from the proverb about the sluggish messenger that such men are very unmeet to be ministers, since Christ will not own the sending of sluggards into his harvest.
themes: a particle that decides between likeness and timing
a promise carried forward into eternity to save it
vinegar read as unripe grapes
a fear fulfilled by the effort to prevent it
hope traced to a root meaning strength

29.pericope_label: The way of the Lord is strength to the upright: the righteous shall never be removed: the mouth of the just bringeth forth wisdom

schools.summary: Henry allows two senses of the way of the Lord, the providence that moves toward us and the godliness appointed for us to walk in, holds that the closer we keep to it the more our hearts are enlarged and that a good conscience gives boldness in a dangerous time, and observes that the wicked would be glad to have this earth their home for ever and cannot.

Gill lists the removals the righteous may undergo, from place to place by persecution, from prosperity to adversity, from comfortable frames of soul and at last out of this world, before naming the one thing they cannot be removed from, and distinguishes men who know what is acceptable from men whose lips know it, the second being practised in saying it.

Clarke makes the way of the Lord a paradox of labour, the more the upright man works the stronger he grows, refers the threat against the froward tongue to the penal cutting out of tongues for blasphemy or treason, quotes his old manuscript Bible for it and adds that extracting the tongue of every scold would leave much less noise in the world, and observes that as the love of God is not in the wicked man’s heart, so the law of kindness is not on his lips; Wesley allows the wicked not so much as a quiet abode on earth, and notes that knowledge is ascribed to the lips as elsewhere to the hands.

Keil and Delitzsch choose the sense of stronghold over that of refuge as the contrast requires, name the way and the fear of the Lord as the two older names of true religion, write an excursus on the peculiar horror of exile to Israel and use the history of the captivity to explain the form of the proverb, trace the verb of the thirty-first verse to a root meaning to spring forth, and refuse both an emendation and a crosswise rearrangement of the closing verses; Ellicott holds that the way of the Lord is itself destruction to the workers of iniquity rather than a place where destruction happens, and makes exile the punishment threatened by the lawgiver and the prophets which fell at last upon the Jews.

debates: Is the way of the Lord merely a place where the wicked meet destruction? Ellicott insists it is destruction to them and not that there is destruction in it, their rejection of the teaching of God being itself their condemnation; Keil and Delitzsch make the same way a bulwark for innocence and ruin for evildoers, choosing the sense of stronghold over that of refuge because the contrast demands it; Henry keeps both a providential and a preceptive sense of the phrase without deciding.

Should the closing verses be emended or rearranged? A critic would change the verb of the last verse and pair the halves of the two closing verses crosswise; Keil and Delitzsch answer that the Greek reading offered in support of the emendation is probably a corruption of another Greek word, that the version cited beside it rests on a manuscript its editor sometimes misread, and that the two halves as they stand fit each other as contrasts, so that the text needs no emendation but only a corrected sense of how the clauses relate.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch write a short excursus on exile, observing that love of home is natural to all but that to no people was fatherland so greatly delighted in, or banishment so dreadful a thought, as to Israel, and that the history of the captivity both confirms this proverb and explains the form it takes.

Ellicott brings the same threat down to his own day, saying that the godless often have to become vagabonds as the first murderer did, and that the punishment threatened by the lawgiver and all the prophets fell at last upon the Jews and is still in force.

Clarke refers the cutting off of the froward tongue to the actual penal practice of cutting out tongues for blasphemy and treasonable speech, and adds that if the tongue of every scold were extracted there would soon be much less noise in the world.
Keil and Delitzsch note that all the old interpreters render the word after the way of the Lord as though a different form stood in the text, while the pointing prefers the abstract.
themes: one road that fortifies and ruins
exile felt as the worst of all threats
words called the fruit of the lips
a tongue cut out in law as well as in metaphor
an emendation refused on the evidence offered for it
